comparator.name: Sociology
comparator.academicYear: Current published UvA bachelor curriculum, checked 2026-09-27
comparator.sourceNotes: The official programme is 180 EC over three years. Year 1 is a fixed 60-EC foundation in sociological theory, institutions, academic craft, philosophy of social science, qualitative and quantitative methodology, statistics and an Amsterdam research project. Year 2 totals 60 EC across four theory/method components and six substantive domains: education and work; intersectionality; migration and citizenship; urban places; health and society; and globalising cultures. Year 3 contains 30 EC genuine free choice, 6 EC Mixed Methods, 6 EC Sociology of Public Policy and an 18-EC Bachelor Research Project culminating in a thesis. The English and bilingual tracks have the same curriculum.
components: Sociological Theory 3: Society, Social Action and Inequality
Genuine open elective space; no minor or elective package is invented.
Independent research culminating in a bachelor thesis within a collaborative project.

alternatives.label: Sociology, inequality & social research
alternatives.concept: Builds a broad sociological programme around theory, institutions, inequality, identity and social change, supported by qualitative inquiry, statistics, data analysis, political economy and an applied research sequence.
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum contains the full available UCR sociology sequence plus inequality, institutions and a substantial qualitative and quantitative research spine.
progression: Introductory sociology, institutions, research and statistics precede modern theory, inequality, qualitative and quantitative analysis, public health, global relations and advanced social research. All prerequisites and planned offerings pass; seven 300-level courses are included.

alternatives.label: Institutions, policy & collective action
alternatives.concept: Examines how political, legal and economic institutions define public problems and shape inequality, policy, organisational diversity, social movements and collective efforts to change society.
alternatives.labelReason: The completed programme is visibly organised around institutions, law, policy, communication and collective action while preserving sociology theory and research methods.
alternatives.distinctness: Compared with the closest programme, this route replaces gender history, experimental statistics, data science and epidemiology with constitutional law, design for public interventions, climate communication and sustainability governance. Those changes follow the policy-and-collective-action concept and meet the four-course distinctness floor.
progression: Sociology, politics, law and research foundations precede comparative institutions, inequality, rights, public communication, governance and collective action. All prerequisites and planned offerings pass; seven 300-level courses are included.

alternatives.label: Migration, race & global society
alternatives.concept: Studies migration, citizenship, race, gender, identity and inequality within globalisation, empire and transnational politics, combining sociological theory with qualitative, historical and political research.
alternatives.labelReason: The completed programme shifts the centre of gravity to migration, race, gender, empire, global political economy and transnational identities while retaining a coherent sociology and research sequence.
alternatives.distinctness: This route replaces most domestic policy, environmental-governance and general quantitative content with histories of empire and gender, international relations and law, global political economy, race, Indigenous histories and political psychology. It differs by at least eight courses from each earlier programme.
progression: Sociology, politics, history and research foundations precede global political economy, migration-related inequality, race, citizenship, identity, international law and advanced transnational analysis. All prerequisites and planned offerings pass; eight 300-level courses are included.

courses: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory

core: Sociological theories of social interaction, institutions, culture, structure and social change
Social inequality across class, race, gender, migration, education, work, health and urban life
Qualitative, quantitative and mixed social research using interviews, ethnography, surveys, statistics and critical evidence assessment
Relationships between individuals, everyday interaction, organisations and wider social structures
Academic sociological craft, theory construction and independent research culminating in a thesis
adjacent: Public policy, social movements and collective responses to societal problems
Migration, citizenship, racism, globalisation and identities shaped by urban and transnational settings
Social organisation of education, work, health and culture
questions: What social structures and mechanisms produce inequality and changing public problems?
How do institutions, policies and collective action reproduce or change social relations?
How can qualitative and quantitative evidence explain social patterns and change?

selection.assessment: The closest programme uses the complete available UCR sociology sequence and a strong mixed-method social-research spine. The institution/policy and migration/race/global-society directions are independently supported by generator-eligible programme interests and the official curriculum, produce substantively different course choices, and pass feasibility and pairwise distinctness. Production therefore stops at the three-alternative maximum.

notes.text: UvA Sociology provides four dedicated theory courses, an integrated quantitative–qualitative methods sequence, six specialist sociological domains and an 18-EC bachelor research project. UCR offers a coherent sociology core and strong related study in politics, law, history, psychology, economics, media and research methods, but it does not reproduce the same continuous specialist sociology sequence. The UCR alternatives therefore preserve this difference in disciplinary depth.
